The clinical presentation centers on progressive, constant, *painless*, *isolated right-arm weakness* over weeks — with no sensory symptoms, no cranial nerve or cerebellar/brainstem involvement, no neck pain, and no observed atrophy. Critically, imaging reveals a right apical lung mass — a classic location for a Pancoast tumor. Pancoast tumors (typically non-small cell lung cancer, especially squamous or adenocarcinoma, though small cell also occurs) commonly invade the lower brachial plexus (C8–T1 roots), producing a *motor-predominant or pure motor neuropathy* affecting hand intrinsics, finger flexors, and thumb abduction — i.e., a *lower trunk brachial plexopathy*. The absence of pain is atypical but not exclusionary: up to ~20% of Pancoast tumors present with *painless* neurologic deficits, especially early or in diabetic or elderly patients. The unintentional 17-pound weight loss strongly supports underlying malignancy. While anti-Hu antibody is ordered (appropriate given paraneoplastic concern), classic anti-Hu–associated syndromes are overwhelmingly *sensory* or *encephalomyelitis*; isolated *pure motor* arm weakness is exceedingly rare with anti-Hu and would be a red herring here without sensory involvement. No evidence supports ALS (no upper motor neuron signs, no bulbar or bilateral involvement, no atrophy), cervical myelopathy (no gait/balance issues, no Lhermitte’s, no sphincter changes), or mononeuritis multiplex (no multifocal asymmetric sensory-motor deficits).
